catalog_quote: 2.1 PHONOLOGY SYLLABLE PATTERNS In Jibə, a syllable consists of two elements: one or more segments and the suprasegmental tone. A segment can be a consonant (C), a vowel (V), or a nasal (N). A tone can be high ( '), mid or low ( ') and is attached to ... [...] 2.4 TONES Jibə has three level tones, which mostly function lexically: Low [ . ], mid [ . ] and high [ . ]. A falling tone [ . ] appears as well, but is of secondary nature, i.e. in vowel sequences of two vowels with different tones, one might be deleted so that a single vowel marked by a falling tone remains. [...] 2.4.1 Examples of lexical tone relevance (12) á-kú "priest; soul" kū "he, she" kù "to fall" mám "to suck" mām "to create" [...] Besides the level tones, the high-low falling tone also occurs in some minimal pairs, e.g.: (13) bá "plural marker" Bâ "personal name"

new_statements.rule_in_words: Jibə (Jiba/Jibe of Kona) is described as a register-tone language: every syllable carries one of three level tones (L, M, H) that are mostly lexically contrastive (minimal pairs kú/kū/kù, mám/mām, kúní/kūní/kúni, jíní/jìní/jini), with a derived HL fall from vowel deletion and some grammatical tone on noun prefixes and pronouns. The sketch has no section on stress or accent and no sentence assigning word stress to any syllable was found; nothing is said about stress at all.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tone: the falling tone is 'of secondary nature' (from two-vowel sequences with different tones) but also appears in a few minimal pairs (bá 'plural marker' vs Bâ 'personal name').
new_statements.domain_note: Syllable- and word-level lexical tone (citation forms in a wordlist-based sketch); grammatical tone on prefixes/pronouns/verbal forms. Evidence is from Google Books snippet view of pp. 27-32 plus the full table of contents, not a full page scan; the words 'stress'/'accent' were not returned in any linguistic sense.
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes 'Jibe' / 'Jibə' = the Jukun of Kona (Kona village, Taraba State), which is exactly Glottolog jiba1237 [juo] (alt. names Jibe, Jibi, Jibə, Jukun Kona, Kona). Not to be confused with Jibu of Serti [jib, jibu1239] or the 'Jibu koine' = Diyi/Jukun Takum [jbu, juku1254]. Meek's 1931 'Kona dialect' (grouped with Gwana and Pindiga = Hone, hone1235) is the same variety.

sources.note: Ch. I 'Linguistics' pp. 1-15: Kona is one of six Jukun dialects ('The dialects of Kona, Gwana, and Pindiga differ so little that they may be regarded as one', p. 1); comparative root table with a Kona column; p. 7 claims 'the Wukari dialect, unlike the other dialects, has a highly developed tonal system' (i.e. Meek thought Kona lacked it; contradicted by Dinslage & Storch's three-tone description); p. 14 'In the Wukari dialect tones are significant'; Kona noted for plural verbs (p. 13) and a voiced velar fricative (p. 14). Nothing on stress or accent for any dialect.
